cards.q: How many questions are on the MLA-C01 exam, and how are they split?
cards.a: 65 total: 50 scored plus 15 unscored. The unscored questions are randomly mixed in and indistinguishable from the scored ones.

cards.q: What is the passing score and scoring model?
cards.a: 720 out of 1,000 on a scaled score. Scoring is compensatory, so there is no minimum you must hit in any single domain.

cards.q: How long is the exam, and what is the guessing strategy?
cards.a: 130 minutes. There is no penalty for wrong answers, so always answer every question rather than leaving any blank.

cards.q: What are the four exam domains and their weights?
cards.a: Data Preparation (28%), ML Model Development (26%), Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows (22%), and ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security (24%).

cards.q: What are the five stages of the ML and AI lifecycle?
cards.a: Frame, prepare, develop, deploy, and operate.

cards.q: What does Amazon SageMaker AI provide within the broader SageMaker platform?
cards.a: Services for building, training, and deploying ML models. The broader SageMaker platform also includes data and analytics capabilities.

cards.q: What does maintenance mode mean in the service lifecycle described by this guide?
cards.a: New customer onboarding is closed while existing customers can continue under the stated support terms, with no new features planned.

cards.q: How does a sunset notice differ from maintenance mode?
cards.a: A sunset notice includes an announced end date that requires migration planning.

cards.q: Which source should take precedence when an old course's service limit conflicts with current AWS documentation?
cards.a: The current official service documentation, checked for the relevant feature and date.

cards.q: What does compensatory exam scoring mean?
cards.a: The overall passing result does not require a separate passing score in every content domain.

cards.q: How does a multiple-response exam question differ from a multiple-choice question?
cards.a: Multiple response requires all requested correct selections; multiple choice has one correct selection.

cards.q: What does MOST cost-effective require beyond choosing the cheapest option?
cards.a: The option must still satisfy every stated requirement.

cards.q: How does LEAST operational overhead differ from LEAST development effort?
cards.a: Operational overhead concerns ongoing work to run and maintain the system; development effort concerns the work needed to implement it.

cards.q: Which question details should guide elimination before comparing product features?
cards.a: The actual requested outcome, the qualifier, and hard constraints such as timing, payload size, access, or permitted operations.

cards.q: Why can a technically true answer option still be wrong?
cards.a: It may solve a different problem, violate a constraint, use the wrong mode, or rely on a false justification.

cards.q: Which file format is best for analytics and ML training queries, and why?
cards.a: Apache Parquet. It is columnar and compressed, and it supports predicate pushdown for efficient queries.

cards.q: What format does SageMaker Pipe mode rely on for large sequential streaming reads?
cards.a: RecordIO — it streams data without staging it locally first.

cards.q: Which format suits streaming ingestion with schema evolution?
cards.a: Apache Avro — row-based and built for schema registry use cases.

cards.q: What is the core difference between Kinesis Data Streams and Data Firehose?
cards.a: Kinesis Data Streams is real-time with custom processing and multiple consumers; Firehose is managed batch delivery to S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch with no coding required.

cards.q: Which service gives you stateful stream processing with windowed aggregations?
cards.a: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink — supports tumbling, sliding, and session windows.

cards.q: Which storage option suits GPU-intensive distributed training that needs very high IOPS?
cards.a: Amazon FSx for Lustre — a high-performance parallel file system that integrates with S3.

cards.q: Which storage lets multiple SageMaker instances mount the same shared file system at once?
cards.a: Amazon EFS, a shared POSIX file system, useful for distributed training with shared data access.

cards.q: What is the difference between StandardScaler and MinMaxScaler?
cards.a: StandardScaler produces zero mean and unit variance; MinMaxScaler rescales values into a 0 to 1 range.

cards.q: When should you use one-hot encoding versus binary encoding?
cards.a: One-hot for low-cardinality nominal features (roughly under 20 categories); binary encoding for high-cardinality features, using log2(N) columns instead of N.

cards.q: What risk does label encoding introduce for non-ordinal categories?
cards.a: It implies a false ordering, which can mislead tree-based models into treating categories as ranked.

cards.q: What is training-serving skew, and how is it fixed?
cards.a: It happens when features are computed differently at training time versus inference time. The fix is a single source of truth, such as SageMaker Feature Store, with an online store for inference and an offline store for training.

cards.q: Name two no-code or low-code AWS tools for data preparation.
cards.a: SageMaker Data Wrangler (inside SageMaker Studio) and AWS Glue DataBrew (aimed at non-technical users).

cards.q: What does the Class Imbalance (CI) bias metric in SageMaker Clarify measure?
cards.a: The ratio of majority-class to minority-class labels, flagging when one class dominates the dataset.

cards.q: How do DPL and KL divergence differ as pre-training bias metrics?
cards.a: DPL measures the difference in positive outcome rates between demographic groups; KL divergence measures the statistical distance between label distributions across groups.

cards.q: Which technique generates synthetic minority-class examples to address class imbalance?
cards.a: SMOTE, the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique.

cards.q: Which service automatically detects PII in data stored in S3?
cards.a: Amazon Macie.

cards.q: How do you enforce data residency for regulated data such as GDPR or PHI?
cards.a: Use AWS Lake Formation with region-specific access policies, combined with S3 bucket policies.

cards.q: What are the three workforce options in SageMaker Ground Truth?
cards.a: Private (your own internal team), vendor (curated third-party labelers), and Amazon Mechanical Turk (public crowdsourced workers).

cards.q: What does Amazon A2I add on top of an AI service prediction?
cards.a: A human review step, triggered when the model confidence score falls below a chosen threshold.

cards.q: How does SageMaker File input mode make training data available?
cards.a: It downloads the dataset to local storage before the training script begins.

cards.q: How does SageMaker FastFile input mode differ from File mode?
cards.a: FastFile reads S3 data on demand through a file interface instead of downloading the entire dataset before training starts.

cards.q: How does SageMaker Pipe input mode deliver training data?
cards.a: It streams data into FIFO named pipes; the training code and input format must support that interface.

cards.q: Which workload characteristics favor FastFile input mode?
cards.a: Large files, mostly sequential reads, and training startup delays caused by downloading the dataset.

cards.q: Why can FSx for Lustre help repeated training over the same S3 dataset?
cards.a: Its high-throughput file system can cache S3-linked data for reuse across training runs.

cards.q: When does EFS fit a training-data workflow particularly well?
cards.a: When the data already resides on a shared, evolving file system and elastic capacity or multi-AZ access matters more than maximum training throughput.

cards.q: What Region constraint applies to a SageMaker training dataset?
cards.a: It must be in the same AWS Region as the training job.

cards.q: What networking must be configured when SageMaker training mounts EFS or FSx for Lustre?
cards.a: VPC connectivity and appropriate access rules; the FSx subnet must also match the file system's Availability Zone.

cards.q: Which data permissions does a training execution role normally need?
cards.a: Read access to training inputs and write access to the designated output location, plus required encryption-key permissions.

cards.q: How can a team identify exactly which objects were used in a training run?
cards.a: Use a manifest and immutable dataset locations or object versions, then record those references with the model.

cards.q: Why can millions of small S3 objects slow training startup?
cards.a: Per-object request overhead dominates. Packing objects into larger shards can reduce that overhead.

cards.q: Why shard a large training dataset across instances instead of replicating it to every instance?
cards.a: Sharding reduces repeated downloads and per-instance storage requirements while supporting distributed training.

cards.q: Why extract a snapshot from an operational database before training?
cards.a: It avoids placing training load on the live database and gives the run a reproducible dataset.

cards.q: Which AWS service fits scheduled transfers from on-premises file systems into AWS storage?
cards.a: AWS DataSync.

cards.q: Why do columnar formats reduce the cost of queries that use only a few features?
cards.a: They allow readers to load selected columns rather than every field of each record.

cards.q: Which file format is a common default for analytical training datasets in S3?
cards.a: Parquet: a columnar format with compression and efficient selective reads.

cards.q: Why is Avro useful when records and schemas evolve in a streaming pipeline?
cards.a: It is a row-oriented binary format that carries schema information with the data.

cards.q: Why can a large gzip-compressed plain-text file limit parallel processing?
cards.a: The compressed file is not normally splittable, so workers cannot independently read arbitrary compressed sections.

cards.q: How do partition pruning and column pruning reduce different parts of a query's work?
cards.a: Partition pruning skips irrelevant data partitions; column pruning skips unneeded columns within the selected data.

cards.q: What is a common downside of over-partitioning a dataset?
cards.a: It creates many small files and increases request, metadata, and scheduling overhead.

cards.q: Why does a poorly distributed Kinesis partition key create a bottleneck?
cards.a: Records for the same key concentrate on one shard, producing a hot shard even when other shards have capacity.

cards.q: What capability makes Kinesis Data Streams suitable for reprocessing events?
cards.a: Its retained, replayable stream lets consumers revisit records within the retention period.

cards.q: When does provisioned Kinesis capacity fit better than automatically managed capacity?
cards.a: When traffic is predictable and the team can manage shard capacity deliberately.

cards.q: What problem does Kinesis enhanced fan-out solve?
cards.a: It gives registered consumers dedicated per-shard read throughput instead of making them compete for shared read capacity.

cards.q: What does Amazon Data Firehose add to a data-delivery pipeline?
cards.a: Managed buffered delivery, with options such as record transformation, format conversion, and dynamic partitioning.

cards.q: Which streaming requirement most strongly favors Data Streams over Firehose?
cards.a: Multiple independent consumers or a need to replay retained events.

cards.q: When is Firehose a strong fit for an ML data-ingestion pipeline?
cards.a: When events need managed buffered delivery to a destination, possibly with format conversion, and replay is not required.

cards.q: Which AWS service fits stateful streaming windows, joins, and aggregations?
cards.a: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink.

cards.q: Why must a stream consumer be idempotent?
cards.a: Records may be delivered more than once; processing a duplicate must not duplicate the intended side effect.

cards.q: How can a pipeline prevent one poison record from blocking a stream shard indefinitely?
cards.a: Limit retries, split failing batches where supported, and send failed records to an appropriate failure destination for investigation.

cards.q: Which AWS service fits large-scale standard ETL with little infrastructure management?
cards.a: AWS Glue.

cards.q: When is a Glue Python shell job more appropriate than a distributed Spark job?
cards.a: For small, single-node Python work that does not justify Spark startup and distribution overhead.

cards.q: What does the Glue Data Catalog store?
cards.a: Metadata such as databases, tables, schemas, and partitions; the underlying data remains in its storage location.

cards.q: What does a Glue crawler automate?
cards.a: Discovery of source schemas and partitions and registration of their metadata in the Data Catalog.

cards.q: What is the purpose of a Glue job bookmark?
cards.a: To track previously processed input so subsequent runs can process new data incrementally.

cards.q: Why do incremental pipelines still need idempotent output writes?
cards.a: Retries or reprocessing of recent partitions must not append duplicate training records.

cards.q: Why are EMR task nodes a common place to use Spot capacity?
cards.a: They add compute without holding HDFS data, reducing the data-loss risk associated with interruptions.

cards.q: What requirement can favor EMR over Glue for transformation work?
cards.a: A required framework version, custom bootstrap libraries, or cluster-level control that the Glue job environment does not provide.

cards.q: When does SageMaker Processing fit better than a separate data-engineering ETL job?
cards.a: When preprocessing belongs to a model's workflow and should use the same libraries and code as training or inference.

cards.q: What distinguishes Data Wrangler's focus from DataBrew's focus?
cards.a: Data Wrangler focuses on ML feature preparation and pipeline export; DataBrew focuses on visual recipes for general data preparation and quality.

cards.q: Why is Lambda unsuitable for an arbitrarily long or distributed transformation?
cards.a: Each invocation is bounded in runtime and resources and does not distribute one invocation across workers.

cards.q: What is a Spark shuffle?
cards.a: Movement of data between executors for operations such as joins and aggregations; it can dominate job cost and latency.

cards.q: What symptom suggests skewed data in a Spark job?
cards.a: Most tasks finish while one or a few tasks continue processing disproportionately large partitions.

cards.q: When can a Spark broadcast join avoid an expensive shuffle?
cards.a: When one joined table is small enough to distribute to the executors.

cards.q: How can separate training and inference preprocessing implementations cause production errors?
cards.a: They can compute different feature values without raising an infrastructure error, creating training-serving skew.

cards.q: What is the safe order for fitting preprocessing and splitting a dataset?
cards.a: Split first, fit transforms on training data only, apply those fitted transforms to validation and test data, and persist them for inference.

cards.q: What is target leakage?
cards.a: A feature exposes the outcome, or information caused by it, that would not be available at prediction time.

cards.q: How can fitting a scaler on the entire dataset contaminate evaluation?
cards.a: The scaler incorporates validation or test statistics into the training process.

cards.q: Why must duplicates be considered before creating train and test sets?
cards.a: The same underlying example can appear in both sets, making memorization look like generalization.

cards.q: Why can a missing-value indicator be useful?
cards.a: Missingness may itself carry predictive information that ordinary imputation would hide.

cards.q: Why is median imputation often preferable to mean imputation for a numeric column with outliers?
cards.a: The median is less sensitive to extreme values.

cards.q: What does min-max normalization do?
cards.a: It rescales values using fitted minimum and maximum values into a chosen range, commonly 0 to 1.

cards.q: What does z-score standardization do?
cards.a: It subtracts the fitted mean and divides by the fitted standard deviation.

cards.q: Which model families are especially sensitive to feature scale?
cards.a: Distance-based models, gradient-based models, and models with coefficient penalties.

cards.q: Why does scaling usually not improve a decision-tree model by itself?
cards.a: Tree splits depend on feature ordering and thresholds rather than distances between differently scaled features.

cards.q: When is one-hot encoding appropriate?
cards.a: For categories with no meaningful order and manageable cardinality.

cards.q: Why can ordinal encoding be misleading for unordered categories?
cards.a: It introduces an artificial numeric order and spacing that the model may interpret as meaningful.

cards.q: Why can target encoding leak labels?
cards.a: The encoded value uses outcome information. It must be learned within training folds rather than from held-out examples.

cards.q: Which encoding keeps a fixed feature width when the number of possible categories is very large or unbounded?
cards.a: Feature hashing, with the trade-off that categories can collide.

cards.q: How should a production encoder handle categories absent from training?
cards.a: Use a deliberate fallback such as an Unknown bucket or, for target encoding, the fitted global mean.

cards.q: Why is multicollinearity a problem for interpreting linear-model coefficients?
cards.a: Correlated predictors can make coefficients unstable and make their individual effects difficult to separate.

cards.q: How does PCA differ from selecting a subset of original features?
cards.a: PCA creates new components from combinations of features; feature selection retains original feature identities.

cards.q: Why should features normally be scaled before PCA?
cards.a: Otherwise, features with larger numeric magnitudes can dominate the components.

cards.q: Which split prevents records from the same customer appearing in both training and test data?
cards.a: A grouped split that keeps each customer's records on one side.

cards.q: Which split preserves minority-class proportions across dataset partitions?
cards.a: A stratified split.

cards.q: Which validation pattern should replace ordinary shuffled k-fold for time-series prediction?
cards.a: Rolling or expanding-window validation that always trains on earlier observations and evaluates on later ones.

cards.q: Which two fields must a SageMaker Feature Store feature group identify?
cards.a: A record identifier and an event-time feature.

cards.q: Why group features by entity rather than creating one feature group per model?
cards.a: Entity-based groups make features reusable across models and help maintain a consistent definition.

cards.q: What are the three basic Feature Store feature data types described in the guide?
cards.a: String, Integral, and Fractional.

cards.q: When is an offline-only feature group sufficient?
cards.a: When features are used for training or batch work and do not require low-latency online lookup.

cards.q: What does using both online and offline feature stores support?
cards.a: Historical feature data for training and current feature values for low-latency inference.

cards.q: What historical-storage limitation applies to the InMemory online tier described in the guide?
cards.a: It supports online-only groups, so it does not replicate a feature history into an offline store.

cards.q: When can provisioned Feature Store throughput fit better than on-demand throughput?
cards.a: When read and write demand is steady and predictable enough to provision capacity economically.

cards.q: Where does the Feature Store offline store keep historical records?
cards.a: In S3, with table metadata that supports analytical queries such as Athena queries.

cards.q: What does DatasetBuilder help produce from multiple feature groups?
cards.a: A joined dataset for training or analysis, including support for point-in-time-correct joins.

cards.q: Why is deleting an online feature record insufficient for erasing its offline history?
cards.a: The offline history may retain prior records and delete markers; the S3-backed history needs separate handling.

cards.q: What maintenance operation makes Iceberg useful for an offline feature store with many small files?
cards.a: Compaction.

cards.q: What does a point-in-time feature join prevent?
cards.a: Using feature values from after a historical label's timestamp, which would leak future information into training.

cards.q: Why might sensitive features belong in their own feature group?
cards.a: It allows access to that group to be restricted independently.

cards.q: How do cross-account online Feature Store reads differ from querying its offline store?
cards.a: Online reads use the Feature Store runtime API and appropriate IAM access; offline reads use the S3 and table-governance path.

cards.q: What is added to a Ground Truth input manifest to create an augmented output manifest?
cards.a: Labels and associated label metadata are attached to the source records.

cards.q: Which workforce type is a natural fit for sensitive data or specialized internal expertise?
cards.a: A private workforce of authorized employees or contractors.

cards.q: What does a custom Ground Truth pre-annotation Lambda do?
cards.a: It prepares the input data for the worker task template before annotation.

cards.q: What does a custom Ground Truth post-annotation Lambda do?
cards.a: It consolidates worker annotations into the resulting label.

cards.q: How does active learning reduce human labeling work?
cards.a: A model labels sufficiently confident examples automatically and sends uncertain examples for human annotation.

cards.q: What should a team investigate when annotators frequently disagree?
cards.a: Ambiguous instructions, unclear examples, or genuinely ambiguous data, before simply adding more reviewers.

cards.q: Why include random human-review samples as well as low-confidence predictions?
cards.a: Random samples can reveal confidently wrong predictions that a confidence threshold would never send for review.

cards.q: What distinguishes Ground Truth's task from Augmented AI's task?
cards.a: Ground Truth creates labels for training data; Augmented AI supports human review of predictions from an operating system.

cards.q: What is an A2I human loop?
cards.a: One instance of a human-review task within a configured review workflow.

cards.q: What does an AWS Glue Data Quality score summarize?
cards.a: The percentage of evaluated quality rules that pass.

cards.q: Which data-quality dimension checks that required fields are present?
cards.a: Completeness.

cards.q: How does a DQDL rule differ from an analyzer?
cards.a: A rule evaluates an expectation; an analyzer gathers statistics without requiring a pass/fail threshold.

cards.q: Where is the guide's ML-powered Glue Data Quality anomaly detection supported?
cards.a: In Glue ETL-based data quality, rather than Data Catalog-based evaluation.

cards.q: What are useful pipeline responses to a failed data-quality rule?
cards.a: Stop downstream processing, quarantine failing rows, or record an informational result, depending on the rule's importance.

cards.q: How does Class Imbalance differ from Difference in Positive Proportions in Labels?
cards.a: Class Imbalance measures representation across groups; DPL compares their positive-label rates.

cards.q: What is the range of the Clarify Class Imbalance metric?
cards.a: From -1 to 1.

cards.q: Why examine conditional demographic disparity as well as overall disparity?
cards.a: Aggregate rates can hide or reverse patterns within subgroups, as in Simpson's paradox.

cards.q: How do class weights address imbalance without resampling data?
cards.a: They change the penalty assigned to errors on different classes during training.

cards.q: Why must SMOTE be applied only after the training split is isolated?
cards.a: Applying it before splitting can place related synthetic examples across training and evaluation sets and inflate performance.

cards.q: What data does Amazon Macie inspect for sensitive information?
cards.a: Data stored in Amazon S3; it is not a general scanner for live training memory or arbitrary databases.

cards.q: What does Lake Formation add beyond object-level S3 permissions?
cards.a: Fine-grained permissions on catalogued data, including table, column, row, and cell-level controls.

cards.q: How does tokenization differ from redaction for sensitive values?
cards.a: Tokenization substitutes a value that can be resolved through a protected mapping; redaction removes the value.

cards.q: Why should hashed or tokenized identifiers not automatically be treated as anonymous data?
cards.a: They can remain linkable or re-identifiable; replacing an identifier does not by itself guarantee anonymity.

cards.q: Why must query and document embeddings use a compatible model and configuration?
cards.a: They must occupy the same vector space for distance or similarity comparisons to be meaningful.

cards.q: What must happen to an embedding when its source text changes?
cards.a: Regenerate it and update the corresponding index entry.

cards.q: What enables a text query to retrieve relevant images through vector search?
cards.a: A multimodal embedding model that represents text and images in a shared vector space.

cards.q: What is the main trade-off when reducing embedding dimensions?
cards.a: Lower storage, memory, and search work in exchange for a possible reduction in retrieval quality.

cards.q: What does cosine similarity emphasize when comparing vectors?
cards.a: Their direction or angle rather than their magnitude.

cards.q: How does Euclidean distance differ from cosine similarity?
cards.a: Euclidean distance measures straight-line separation and is affected by vector magnitude.

cards.q: What does an approximate nearest-neighbor index trade for faster search?
cards.a: Some probability of finding the exact nearest neighbors.

cards.q: What is the basic structure used by HNSW vector indexes?
cards.a: A navigable graph connecting vectors to support efficient neighbor search.

cards.q: What does increasing an ANN search's breadth typically do?
cards.a: It can improve retrieval recall while increasing computation and latency.

cards.q: What is the purpose of Amazon S3 Vectors?
cards.a: Managed storage and similarity search for vectors using vector buckets and indexes.

cards.q: Which S3 vector-index choices require particular care before index creation?
cards.a: Vector dimensions, distance metric, and the declared non-filterable metadata configuration.

cards.q: What problem does hybrid keyword and vector search address?
cards.a: Keywords help match exact identifiers; vectors help match semantic meaning and paraphrases.

cards.q: When can PostgreSQL with pgvector be attractive compared with adding a separate vector service?
cards.a: When vectors need to stay close to existing relational records and be queried or joined through SQL.

cards.q: Why should authorization attributes be stored with vector-search metadata?
cards.a: They allow retrieval to restrict results to documents the requesting user is permitted to access.

cards.q: What is a security trade-off between a per-tenant index and one shared index?
cards.a: Separate indexes support resource-level isolation; a shared index depends on consistently enforced tenant filtering.

cards.q: Why should embeddings receive protection similar to their source documents?
cards.a: Vectors and associated metadata can disclose sensitive source information; embedding is not anonymization.

cards.q: What operational consequence follows from changing an embedding model?
cards.a: The corpus usually needs to be re-embedded and its vector index rebuilt for the new space.

cards.q: What is the fundamental difference between fixed-size and semantic chunking?
cards.a: Fixed-size chunking targets a token size; semantic chunking seeks boundaries where the topic or meaning changes.

cards.q: Why add overlap between adjacent document chunks?
cards.a: To preserve information that spans a chunk boundary.

cards.q: What is the downside of excessive chunk overlap?
cards.a: More embedding and storage work and more near-duplicate retrieval results.

cards.q: How can chunk size increase recurring RAG inference costs?
cards.a: Retrieved chunks become prompt context, so larger chunks can add input tokens to every request.

cards.q: Why can semantic chunking cost more during ingestion than fixed-size chunking?
cards.a: It performs semantic analysis, including embedding-based comparisons, to choose boundaries.

cards.q: How does hierarchical chunking combine search precision with broader context?
cards.a: It searches smaller child chunks and returns larger parent chunks containing them.

cards.q: Why might hierarchical retrieval return fewer results than the requested count?
cards.a: Several matching children can be replaced by the same parent chunk.

cards.q: When is no chunking appropriate for a knowledge-base data source?
cards.a: When each file is already a small, coherent retrieval unit, or when custom preprocessing produces those units.

cards.q: Can the configured chunking strategy of an existing Bedrock data source simply be edited?
cards.a: No. The guide describes creating a new data source and re-ingesting to change the strategy.

cards.q: Why might a default text parser be inadequate for a visually complex PDF?
cards.a: It may not preserve the information in images, tables, figures, or their reading order.

cards.q: What are Bedrock Data Automation blueprints used for?
cards.a: Defining the fields and output structure to extract for a document type.

cards.q: What requirement favors transcription-oriented parsing over purely visual similarity search for meeting recordings?
cards.a: Finding what participants said, rather than finding visually similar scenes.

cards.q: Why should table headers remain associated with their rows during RAG preparation?
cards.a: Values lose their meaning when chunking or text flattening separates them from the column definitions.

cards.q: When should document permissions enter a RAG pipeline?
cards.a: Capture them during ingestion as filterable metadata and enforce them during retrieval.

cards.q: Which metadata supports traceable citations in generated answers?
cards.a: Source document identifiers and locations such as pages or sections.

cards.q: Why can deleting a source file fail to remove it immediately from RAG results?
cards.a: The knowledge base may still contain its indexed chunks until the relevant ingestion or synchronization process handles the deletion.

cards.q: What is JSONL's record structure for a model-customization dataset?
cards.a: One JSON object per line, with the fields and schema required by the chosen model and customization method.

cards.q: What should be checked in a supervised fine-tuning prompt-response pair?
cards.a: That the response correctly answers its own prompt and follows the intended quality and formatting requirements.

cards.q: Why count tokens rather than characters before submitting fine-tuning records?
cards.a: Model limits apply to tokens, and character counts are an unreliable proxy.

cards.q: What does decreasing training loss alongside increasing validation loss suggest?
cards.a: Overfitting; consider stopping earlier and selecting an earlier checkpoint.

cards.q: What kind of training data is associated with continued pre-training?
cards.a: A large domain corpus rather than a collection of ideal task-specific responses.

cards.q: What are the teacher and student roles in model distillation?
cards.a: The teacher supplies useful behavior or responses; a smaller student is trained to reproduce that behavior at lower serving cost.

cards.q: Must Bedrock distillation always begin with a manually authored prompt-only file?
cards.a: No. The documentation notes also describe labeled examples and invocation logs as supported inputs.

cards.q: What does preference data record?
cards.a: A comparison or ranking of alternative responses rather than only one ideal response.

cards.q: How does DPO differ from the reward-model approach described for RLHF?
cards.a: DPO optimizes from preference pairs directly, without first training a separate reward model.

cards.q: Why screen production invocation logs before using them for distillation?
cards.a: They may contain personal data, sensitive content, or examples unsuitable for the intended training use.

cards.q: What is catastrophic forgetting during customization?
cards.a: Improved performance on a narrow task comes with deterioration of previously learned capabilities.

cards.q: How can a team reduce catastrophic forgetting risk?
cards.a: Use representative general examples, conservative training settings, and evaluation beyond the narrow target task.

cards.q: What is the central idea of parameter-efficient fine-tuning such as LoRA?
cards.a: Train a small subset of added or selected parameters while keeping most base-model weights fixed.

cards.q: Several models need the same historical customer features and current online values. Which shared capability best fits?
cards.a: Feature Store, rather than independently recomputing and maintaining the same features for every model.

cards.q: What correction does the dated documentation note make to the slide's Mechanical Turk lifecycle claim?
cards.a: Mechanical Turk permanently closed on September 30, 2026; it was not merely continuing in maintenance.

cards.q: Which SageMaker built-in algorithm is the go-to for tabular classification and regression?
cards.a: XGBoost — gradient boosted trees, considered the industry standard for structured data.

cards.q: What does SageMaker Linear Learner support?
cards.a: Linear and logistic regression at scale: binary classification, multiclass classification, and regression.

cards.q: When would you use the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm?
cards.a: For classification or regression based on nearby examples. It is a simple baseline model.

cards.q: What does the K-Means algorithm do?
cards.a: Unsupervised clustering: it groups unlabelled data into K clusters based on similarity.

cards.q: What is Principal Component Analysis (PCA) used for?
cards.a: Unsupervised dimensionality reduction. It reduces the feature space before training by projecting data onto principal components.

cards.q: What does the DeepAR algorithm do?
cards.a: Probabilistic time-series forecasting using RNNs, designed for multiple related time series at once.

cards.q: What are the two main uses of BlazingText?
cards.a: Word2Vec word embeddings and text classification. It is optimized for fast training on large text corpora.

cards.q: Which tasks suit the Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) algorithm?
cards.a: Machine translation and text summarisation. Its encoder-decoder architecture maps an input sequence to an output sequence.

cards.q: What does Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) do?
cards.a: Unsupervised topic modelling for text corpora. It represents documents as mixtures of topics and topics as distributions over words.

cards.q: What is Random Cut Forest used for?
cards.a: Unsupervised anomaly detection, especially for spotting outliers in streaming data.

cards.q: What is the IP Insights algorithm used for?
cards.a: Unsupervised anomaly detection for IP address usage patterns, such as unusual IP addresses associated with a user or account.

cards.q: What does Object2Vec learn, and where is it useful?
cards.a: Embeddings for pairs of objects, such as users and items. These representations support recommendations and similarity prediction.

cards.q: What does the SageMaker Image Classification algorithm predict?
cards.a: Image-level labels using a convolutional neural network (CNN). It supports multi-label classification, so an image can receive more than one label.

cards.q: How does the built-in Object Detection algorithm locate objects?
cards.a: It detects and classifies objects using bounding boxes. The MXNet implementation uses Single Shot Detector (SSD) with a backbone such as ResNet.

cards.q: How does Semantic Segmentation differ from image classification?
cards.a: Semantic Segmentation assigns a class to every pixel. Image classification assigns labels to the image as a whole.

cards.q: What is TabTransformer designed for?
cards.a: Transformer-based classification and regression on tabular data with heterogeneous categorical and numerical features. It learns contextual embeddings for categorical features.

cards.q: Which AWS AI service extracts text, forms, and tables from scanned PDFs and images?
cards.a: Amazon Textract.

cards.q: How does Amazon Comprehend differ from Amazon Rekognition?
cards.a: Comprehend provides NLP: sentiment, entity recognition, key phrase extraction, topic modelling, and PII detection. Rekognition analyzes images and video for objects, faces, and content moderation.

cards.q: Which AWS service converts audio to text using automatic speech recognition (ASR)?
cards.a: Amazon Transcribe.

cards.q: Which AWS service provides neural machine translation between languages?
cards.a: Amazon Translate.

cards.q: Which AWS service converts text to speech in multiple voices and languages?
cards.a: Amazon Polly.

cards.q: Which AWS service provides managed recommendations without requiring ML expertise?
cards.a: Amazon Personalize — a managed recommendation engine for personalized user experiences.

cards.q: What is Amazon Fraud Detector used for?
cards.a: Managed ML fraud detection using transaction and event data. AWS stopped accepting new customers on November 7, 2025; existing customers can continue using the service.

cards.q: Which AWS service provides intelligent enterprise search using NLP?
cards.a: Amazon Kendra — searches enterprise content to find relevant information and answers.

cards.q: What does Amazon Lex provide?
cards.a: Conversational AI for voice and text chatbots using automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding. It uses the same deep learning technology that powers Amazon Alexa.

cards.q: What does Amazon Bedrock provide for generative AI applications?
cards.a: Managed access to foundation models (FMs) for text, image, and multimodal tasks, with support for model fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

cards.q: What is the difference between an epoch and a training step?
cards.a: An epoch is one full pass through the dataset; a step is one gradient update. Total steps ≈ (epochs × dataset size) / batch size; rounding depends on how partial batches are handled.

cards.q: How does batch size affect training updates?
cards.a: Batch size is the number of examples per gradient update. Larger batches usually give more stable, less noisy gradients; smaller batches give more updates per epoch and more stochastic gradients.

cards.q: What does the learning rate control?
cards.a: The step size in gradient descent. Too high can cause oscillation or divergence; too low can slow convergence or leave training stuck near a local minimum or plateau.

cards.q: What is dropout, and why is it used?
cards.a: A neural-network regularization technique that randomly disables a fraction of units during training. It reduces co-adaptation and overfitting; dropout is disabled during inference.

cards.q: How does data parallelism differ from model parallelism?
cards.a: Data parallelism replicates the full model on each device, splits the data, and averages gradients; it suits models that fit on one GPU. Model parallelism splits layers or parameters across devices for oversized models, such as very large LLMs.

cards.q: What is pipeline parallelism?
cards.a: An extension of model parallelism: split the model into stages across devices and pipeline micro-batches through them. Overlapping stage execution reduces GPU idle time.

cards.q: How do you tell overfitting apart from underfitting using loss curves?
cards.a: Low training loss with high validation loss signals overfitting. High loss on both training and validation signals underfitting.

cards.q: What do training and validation losses look like with good generalisation?
cards.a: Both losses are low and close together, indicating that the model performs well on training data and held-out validation data.

cards.q: Name a few common ways to fix overfitting.
cards.a: Reduce model complexity, add regularization such as L1, L2, or dropout, use early stopping, gather more training data, or apply feature selection and data augmentation.

cards.q: How can model complexity and training data be adjusted to reduce overfitting?
cards.a: Use fewer layers, lower max_depth, or fewer estimators where appropriate. Collect more training data, remove noisy or irrelevant features, and use data augmentation to artificially expand training data.

cards.q: How does early stopping help prevent overfitting?
cards.a: Monitor validation loss and stop training when it stops improving, usually after a patience period. Keep the checkpoint with the best validation performance.

cards.q: What are common ways to fix underfitting?
cards.a: Increase model complexity, train longer with more epochs, reduce regularization strength, and engineer more informative features.

cards.q: How can learning rate decay contribute to underfitting?
cards.a: If the learning rate decays too quickly, updates may become too small before the model has learned enough. Reduce the decay or slow the schedule so learning can continue.

cards.q: What is catastrophic forgetting, and how is it addressed?
cards.a: It occurs when fine-tuning on a new task erases previously learned knowledge. Mitigations include Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), learning-rate warm-up, or freezing early layers, depending on the task.

cards.q: What is the key practical difference between L1 and L2 regularization?
cards.a: L1 (Lasso) can drive weights to zero, producing sparsity for feature selection. L2 (Ridge) shrinks weights toward zero and suits correlated features. Weight decay is a related regularization approach used in neural networks.

cards.q: How does grid search work, and what is its main limitation?
cards.a: It exhaustively evaluates every combination in a grid, finding the best tested configuration for the chosen metric. Trial count grows multiplicatively with values per hyperparameter, making large search spaces impractical.

cards.q: When is random search useful for hyperparameter tuning?
cards.a: It randomly samples configurations from the search space. It scales better than exhaustive grid search and is effective for wide initial exploration with a limited trial budget.

cards.q: Which hyperparameter tuning strategy is the default in SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning, and how does it work?
cards.a: Bayesian optimization builds a probabilistic surrogate model and uses an acquisition function to select the next promising configuration. It often finds good settings in fewer trials, though efficiency depends on the problem.

cards.q: What is Hyperband best suited for?
cards.a: Multi-fidelity tuning of iterative models, especially neural networks with early stopping. It briefly trains many configurations, eliminates poor performers, and allocates more training resources to promising survivors.

cards.q: What does SageMaker Neo do?
cards.a: It compiles and quantizes trained models for specific hardware targets, shrinking model size and improving inference latency at the edge.

cards.q: What is the core difference between bagging and boosting?
cards.a: Bagging trains models independently on bootstrapped data subsets to reduce variance, as in Random Forest. Boosting trains models sequentially so each corrects the previous one, reducing bias, as in XGBoost.

cards.q: When should precision be prioritized over recall, or vice versa?
cards.a: Prioritize precision when false positives are costly, such as spam detection. Prioritize recall when false negatives are costly, such as disease detection.

cards.q: What does AUC-ROC actually measure?
cards.a: How well the model discriminates between classes across every possible decision threshold — it is threshold-independent.

cards.q: Between RMSE and MAE, which is more sensitive to outliers?
cards.a: RMSE, because it squares the errors. MAE is more robust to outliers since it uses absolute values.

cards.q: What does SageMaker Debugger do during training?
cards.a: It captures training tensors and raises rules automatically for issues like vanishing or exploding gradients, overfitting, or poor weight initialization.

cards.q: How does SageMaker File mode differ from Pipe mode?
cards.a: File mode downloads the entire dataset locally before training starts. Pipe mode streams data directly from S3 in RecordIO or TFRecord format, giving a faster start on very large datasets.

cards.q: When should a deterministic rule be preferred to an ML model?
cards.a: When the required behavior can be expressed reliably as a rule and does not require learning a complex or changing pattern from data.

cards.q: What is Amazon Bedrock's main role in a foundation-model application?
cards.a: It provides managed access to foundation models through APIs, with capabilities for customization, retrieval, evaluation, and safeguards.

cards.q: Which AWS service fits extracting printed fields and tables from scanned forms without training a model?
cards.a: Amazon Textract.

cards.q: What principle should guide the choice between a managed AI capability and custom model training?
cards.a: Choose the most managed option that meets the requirements; add customization or custom training only when needed.

cards.q: When is RAG a better fit than fine-tuning for an internal policy assistant?
cards.a: When answers depend on frequently changing documents, need citations, or must respect document-level access.

cards.q: What kind of requirement most directly favors fine-tuning over retrieval?
cards.a: A stable need to change model behavior, such as a particular output format, style, or task-specific response pattern.

cards.q: How does few-shot prompting differ from zero-shot prompting?
cards.a: Few-shot prompting includes examples of the desired behavior; zero-shot prompting relies on instructions without examples.

cards.q: Why treat a production prompt as a versioned artifact?
cards.a: A prompt change can alter behavior, so its version should be testable, traceable, and reversible.

cards.q: Which request pattern benefits most from prompt caching?
cards.a: Repeated requests that share a substantial, cacheable prompt prefix.

cards.q: What does intelligent prompt routing try to optimize?
cards.a: The choice of model for a request so that suitable quality can be achieved at an appropriate cost.

cards.q: Why check data-residency requirements before using cross-Region inference?
cards.a: The inference profile may route requests to Regions outside the application's permitted processing locations.

cards.q: What does SageMaker JumpStart provide for model development?
cards.a: Pretrained models and supporting resources that can be deployed or adapted instead of starting from scratch.

cards.q: How should candidate modeling approaches be compared in a small proof of concept?
cards.a: Use the same representative evaluation cases and criteria, including difficult examples.

cards.q: Which SageMaker capability fits an analyst building models through a visual interface?
cards.a: SageMaker Canvas.

cards.q: Why is an FM's written explanation insufficient evidence of why it produced an answer?
cards.a: A plausible generated rationale may not faithfully describe the process that produced the response.

cards.q: Why are prompt changes generally cheaper to reverse than embedding-model changes?
cards.a: A prompt can be versioned and rolled back; an embedding-model change can require re-embedding the entire corpus.

cards.q: Which SageMaker built-in algorithm is a common starting point for tabular classification or regression?
cards.a: XGBoost.

cards.q: What trade-off does XGBoost max_depth control?
cards.a: Deeper trees can represent more complex patterns but increase overfitting risk.

cards.q: How does lowering XGBoost eta affect training?
cards.a: It reduces each boosting step's contribution and often requires more boosting rounds.

cards.q: Which XGBoost setting is a direct lever for weighting the positive class in an imbalanced problem?
cards.a: scale_pos_weight.

cards.q: When can Linear Learner be attractive for a tabular problem?
cards.a: When a fast, compact linear or logistic model and interpretable coefficients fit the requirements.

cards.q: What type of data particularly suits Factorization Machines?
cards.a: High-dimensional sparse features with useful pairwise interactions, such as user-item recommendation data.

cards.q: What advantage does DeepAR gain from training on related time series together?
cards.a: It learns shared patterns that can help forecast individual series with limited history.

cards.q: What does DeepAR prediction_length specify?
cards.a: How many future time steps the model forecasts.

cards.q: What distinguishes a probabilistic forecast from a single point forecast?
cards.a: It represents uncertainty through a predictive distribution or quantiles.

cards.q: What are the two main BlazingText modes described in the guide?
cards.a: Word2Vec word embeddings and supervised text classification.

cards.q: Which built-in algorithm fits learning representations from pairs of related objects?
cards.a: Object2Vec.

cards.q: What task do LDA and Neural Topic Model address?
cards.a: Discovering latent topics in an unlabeled collection of documents.

cards.q: Which K-Means choice must be supplied rather than discovered automatically by the algorithm?
cards.a: The number of clusters, k.

cards.q: Which SageMaker built-in algorithm assigns unsupervised anomaly scores to observations?
cards.a: Random Cut Forest.

cards.q: What specialized anomaly-detection problem does IP Insights address?
cards.a: Whether an entity, such as an account, is using an IPv4 address inconsistent with its learned usage patterns.

cards.q: How do image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation differ in their outputs?
cards.a: Classification labels an image; detection labels and locates objects with boxes; segmentation assigns classes at pixel level.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the model input channel in supported incremental-training workflows?
cards.a: It supplies a previously trained model artifact from which training can continue.

cards.q: When does script mode fit better than configuring a built-in algorithm?
cards.a: When the training logic needs behavior such as a custom loss, metric, or preprocessing step.

cards.q: In SageMaker script mode, what does SM_CHANNEL_TRAIN identify?
cards.a: The local path where the training input channel is made available.

cards.q: Where should a training script write model artifacts for SageMaker to package and upload?
cards.a: The directory identified by SM_MODEL_DIR.

cards.q: When does data parallelism address the training bottleneck?
cards.a: When the model fits on each device but training needs more throughput by processing different data shards concurrently.

cards.q: When is model parallelism needed rather than simply replicating the model?
cards.a: When the model or its required training state cannot fit on one device.

cards.q: What does SageMaker Distributed Data Parallel optimize?
cards.a: Collective communication used to synchronize distributed training, such as AllReduce and AllGather.

cards.q: Why can EFA help distributed training scale?
cards.a: It reduces communication latency and supports high-throughput inter-instance communication.

cards.q: What training setting should be reconsidered when scaling the global batch size across more devices?
cards.a: The learning rate and related optimization settings, because convergence behavior can change.

cards.q: How does tensor parallelism differ from pipeline parallelism?
cards.a: Tensor parallelism splits work within layers; pipeline parallelism assigns different layers or stages to different devices.

cards.q: How does gradient accumulation reduce the memory needed for a target effective batch size?
cards.a: It accumulates gradients from several smaller microbatches before applying an update.

cards.q: What kind of training workload is SageMaker HyperPod designed to support?
cards.a: Long-running, large-scale training on persistent clusters with recovery from infrastructure failures.

cards.q: Why is checkpointing central to cost-effective Managed Spot Training?
cards.a: An interruption can resume useful work from saved state instead of repeating the entire run.

cards.q: How do MaxRuntimeInSeconds and MaxWaitTimeInSeconds differ for Managed Spot Training?
cards.a: MaxRuntime limits training runtime; MaxWait includes the time allowed for waiting on Spot capacity.

cards.q: What must a script do beyond writing checkpoints to make resumption work?
cards.a: Detect a restored checkpoint, load the relevant training state, and continue rather than always starting over.

cards.q: Which run inputs should be recorded for reproducible training?
cards.a: The dataset version, container image version, code version, hyperparameters, and relevant random seeds.

cards.q: What do SageMaker managed warm pools save, and what do they cost?
cards.a: They reduce repeated infrastructure provisioning time, but retained resources remain billable.

cards.q: Why does an isolated training container need its dependencies prepared in advance?
cards.a: It cannot download packages through ordinary outbound network access at runtime.

cards.q: Why can automatic model tuning receive no objective metric from an otherwise running script?
cards.a: The configured metric-extraction expression may not match the values printed by the script.

cards.q: Why should hyperparameter tuning optimize a validation metric rather than a training metric?
cards.a: A training metric rewards fitting the training examples and can select an overfit model.

cards.q: Which tuning parameter types represent a numeric range, whole numbers, and a fixed set of choices?
cards.a: Continuous, integer, and categorical parameters, respectively.

cards.q: When is logarithmic scaling appropriate for a hyperparameter search range?
cards.a: When meaningful changes span orders of magnitude, as with learning rates or regularization strengths.

cards.q: How does Bayesian hyperparameter optimization use completed trials?
cards.a: It uses their results to choose promising settings for later trials.

cards.q: Why is random search straightforward to parallelize?
cards.a: Trials are selected independently rather than waiting to learn from previous trial outcomes.

cards.q: How does Hyperband reduce tuning work?
cards.a: It uses intermediate performance to stop weak runs early and allocate more resources to promising runs.

cards.q: What makes a training workload suitable for Hyperband?
cards.a: Runs are costly enough for early termination to help and expose intermediate metrics that support comparison.

cards.q: How do max_jobs and max_parallel_jobs control a tuning job?
cards.a: max_jobs limits the total number of trials; max_parallel_jobs limits how many run concurrently.

cards.q: Why can excessive parallelism reduce Bayesian search efficiency?
cards.a: Many trials are chosen before results from earlier trials become available.

cards.q: What does warm start reuse in automatic model tuning?
cards.a: Evaluation results from eligible parent tuning jobs.

cards.q: What error pattern suggests underfitting?
cards.a: Both training and validation errors remain high.

cards.q: What error pattern suggests overfitting?
cards.a: Training error is low while validation error is substantially higher.

cards.q: How does L1 regularization support feature selection?
cards.a: Its penalty can drive some coefficients exactly to zero.

cards.q: How does L2 regularization usually affect model weights?
cards.a: It shrinks weights smoothly rather than typically eliminating features with exact zeros.

cards.q: When is dropout applied in a neural network?
cards.a: During training; the full network is used for inference.

cards.q: What changes can address underfitting?
cards.a: More suitable features, additional model capacity or training, or less restrictive regularization.

cards.q: What does the temperature parameter control in text generation?
cards.a: The concentration of the sampling distribution and therefore the degree of output randomness.

cards.q: What does topP control?
cards.a: The cumulative probability mass from which the next token may be sampled.

cards.q: Does temperature zero guarantee identical model outputs?
cards.a: No. Serving behavior, numerical effects, and model-version changes can still introduce variation.

cards.q: Where are model-specific Converse parameters such as topK supplied?
cards.a: Through additionalModelRequestFields when the chosen model supports them, rather than the common inferenceConfig fields.

cards.q: What should be checked when a generated answer stops before completing its task?
cards.a: The response's stop reason, the maxTokens setting, and any configured stop sequences.

cards.q: What is the main benefit of the Bedrock Converse API?
cards.a: A consistent message-based interface across models that support it.

cards.q: Who maintains the conversation history for successive Converse requests?
cards.a: The application maintains and sends the relevant messages; each request is stateless.

cards.q: How can an application keep a long conversation within a model's context window?
cards.a: Trim older turns or summarize them while preserving necessary instructions and recent context.

cards.q: What does time to first token measure?
cards.a: How long a user waits before the first generated token becomes available.

cards.q: Does the model itself execute a tool call returned by Converse?
cards.a: No. Application code validates and executes the requested tool and returns its result to the model.

cards.q: What information should a tool definition provide to the model?
cards.a: A clear name, purpose, and input schema.

cards.q: Why does prompt injection become more serious when a model has tools?
cards.a: Untrusted instructions can influence actions as well as generated text.

cards.q: Why validate model-generated structured output even when a schema was requested?
cards.a: The response can still violate syntax, schema, or application-level constraints.

cards.q: What requirement favors tool use rather than RAG over a static document collection?
cards.a: Access to live system state or an action that must be executed in an external system.

cards.q: Which Bedrock invocation path does the guide specify for Custom Model Import?
cards.a: Use the supported Invoke API path; the guide states imported models are not supported by Converse.

cards.q: What is a false positive in a binary classifier?
cards.a: An actually negative example that the model predicts as positive.

cards.q: What is a false negative in a binary classifier?
cards.a: An actually positive example that the model predicts as negative.

cards.q: What is the formula for precision?
cards.a: TP / (TP + FP): the proportion of predicted positives that are actually positive.

cards.q: What is the formula for recall?
cards.a: TP / (TP + FN): the proportion of actual positives that the model finds.

cards.q: Which metric deserves particular attention when false alarms make an action expensive or disruptive?
cards.a: Precision, while checking that recall remains acceptable.

cards.q: Which metric deserves particular attention when missing a positive case is especially costly?
cards.a: Recall, while checking the resulting false-alarm burden.

cards.q: How is F1 calculated from precision and recall?
cards.a: 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall), their harmonic mean.

cards.q: What does choosing an F-beta score with beta greater than 1 emphasize?
cards.a: Recall more strongly than precision.

cards.q: What generally happens to recall when a classifier's positive-decision threshold is lowered?
cards.a: Recall rises or stays the same because more examples are classified as positive; false positives may also increase.

cards.q: What does it mean for predicted probabilities to be calibrated?
cards.a: Among examples assigned probability p, approximately proportion p actually experience the event.

cards.q: How can a cost matrix guide threshold selection?
cards.a: Assign costs to correct and incorrect decisions, then choose a threshold that minimizes expected business cost on representative validation data.

cards.q: What does a ROC curve plot?
cards.a: True positive rate against false positive rate as the decision threshold changes.

cards.q: Why is PR-AUC often more informative than ROC-AUC for a very rare positive class?
cards.a: It focuses on precision and recall for the positive class instead of benefiting from many true negatives.

cards.q: Why choose RMSE over MAE when large prediction errors are particularly undesirable?
cards.a: Squaring errors before averaging gives large errors more influence; the square root returns the metric to the target's units.

cards.q: Why can MAPE be misleading when actual values are zero or near zero?
cards.a: Percentage errors divide by the actual value, making them undefined or excessively large.

cards.q: Which loss fits evaluating a particular quantile of a probabilistic forecast?
cards.a: Quantile loss.

cards.q: Which ranking metric rewards placing highly relevant results nearer the top of a list?
cards.a: NDCG.

cards.q: What does a negative R-squared value indicate on an evaluation set?
cards.a: The predictions perform worse than using the target mean as the baseline under the R-squared calculation.

cards.q: Why use a macro-averaged metric when rare classes matter?
cards.a: It gives each class equal weight rather than allowing large classes to dominate.

cards.q: Why report evaluation results by segment as well as overall?
cards.a: A strong average can conceal unacceptable performance for a particular group, region, or other segment.

cards.q: Why should the test set be separated from validation data used for model selection?
cards.a: Repeated development decisions adapt to validation data; a separate untouched test set supports a final performance estimate.

cards.q: How can SageMaker Pipelines prevent registration of a model that misses a quality threshold?
cards.a: Use a ConditionStep to inspect an evaluation metric and register the model only on the passing branch.

cards.q: What type of similarity does BLEU primarily measure?
cards.a: N-gram overlap with reference text, emphasizing precision and including a brevity penalty.

cards.q: What does ROUGE primarily assess in a generated summary?
cards.a: How much reference content is covered through overlap-based measures, often emphasizing recall.

cards.q: Why can BERTScore reward a valid paraphrase that BLEU penalizes?
cards.a: It compares contextual semantic representations rather than requiring the same words.

cards.q: Why does a high semantic-similarity score not establish factual correctness?
cards.a: Semantically similar statements can make different or false factual claims.

cards.q: What does perplexity measure rather than directly establishing answer quality?
cards.a: How surprising a text is to the language model under its probability distribution.

cards.q: What does an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator do?
cards.a: It scores responses against defined criteria using another model, often with an explanation of the rating.

cards.q: Why calibrate an LLM judge against human ratings?
cards.a: The judge can have style, verbosity, family, or domain biases that do not match the intended quality standard.

cards.q: Why should a tiny difference between two judge-scored systems be treated cautiously?
cards.a: Judge variance and a small evaluation sample can make the difference statistical noise.

cards.q: Which RAG evaluation isolates whether the retriever found useful passages?
cards.a: Retrieve-only evaluation.

cards.q: How does context relevance differ from context coverage?
cards.a: Relevance asks whether retrieved passages are pertinent; coverage asks whether they contain enough information to answer the question.

cards.q: What does faithfulness measure in a RAG answer?
cards.a: Whether the generated claims are supported by the retrieved context.

cards.q: Can a faithful answer still be factually wrong?
cards.a: Yes. It can accurately reflect retrieved material that is itself incorrect or outdated.

cards.q: Why inspect citation quality rather than checking only that citations exist?
cards.a: A citation must actually support the associated claim; an authoritative-looking link can still be irrelevant.

cards.q: What cases should a generative-system evaluation set include beyond ordinary successful requests?
cards.a: Difficult, ambiguous, multipart, out-of-scope, and appropriate-refusal cases.

cards.q: Which changes should trigger regression evaluation of a RAG application?
cards.a: Changes to its model, prompts, retrieval configuration, or knowledge-base content that may affect behavior.

cards.q: Why evaluate an agent's trajectory as well as its final answer?
cards.a: A correct result can hide unsafe actions, unnecessary tool calls, loops, or excessive cost.

cards.q: What does the sign of a SHAP attribution indicate?
cards.a: Whether a feature pushes a prediction above or below the selected baseline.

cards.q: How does a local explanation differ from a global explanation?
cards.a: A local explanation addresses one prediction; a global explanation summarizes behavior across examples.

cards.q: Why does the baseline matter in a SHAP explanation?
cards.a: Attributions are contributions relative to that baseline, so changing it can change the interpretation.

cards.q: What does a partial dependence plot show?
cards.a: The average relationship between a selected feature and the model's predictions as that feature varies.

cards.q: Why can a partial dependence plot mislead when predictors are strongly correlated?
cards.a: Varying one feature independently can evaluate combinations that are unrealistic in the actual data.

cards.q: Why can post-training bias checks reveal problems absent from pre-training label checks?
cards.a: The trained model can produce unequal outcomes or errors even when the training labels show no corresponding disparity.

cards.q: What does disparate impact compare in predicted outcomes?
cards.a: The ratio of positive prediction rates between groups.

cards.q: What information should an experiment-tracking record preserve?
cards.a: Parameters, metrics, artifacts, and the exact data and software versions needed to interpret and reproduce the run.

cards.q: What role does managed MLflow play in a SageMaker workflow?
cards.a: Tracking and comparing runs, metrics, parameters, and artifacts through an MLflow interface integrated with SageMaker.

cards.q: What question does model lineage answer during an incident investigation?
cards.a: Which data, code, training job, and model version produced the deployed behavior.

cards.q: What should a model card document?
cards.a: Intended use, limitations and risks, training details, and evaluation evidence.

cards.q: What end-of-support date does the documentation note give for SageMaker Profiler?
What open-source technique can provide feature attributions when Clarify is unavailable to a new customer?
cards.a: SHAP, integrated into an owned evaluation or monitoring workflow.

cards.q: Which SageMaker endpoint type suits large payloads (up to 1GB) with long processing times?
cards.a: Asynchronous Inference — requests are queued in SQS and results are written to S3.

cards.q: When should you choose Serverless Inference over a real-time endpoint?
cards.a: When traffic is sporadic or unpredictable. It scales to zero with no idle cost, though cold starts are possible.

cards.q: What is a Multi-Model Endpoint (MME) best suited for?
cards.a: Hosting many low-traffic models that share the same framework on shared compute, which can cut costs by up to 90%.

cards.q: Which metric should drive SageMaker endpoint auto scaling, and why not CPU utilization?
cards.a: SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance — CPU utilization lags behind the actual inference load.

cards.q: How does a canary deployment differ from blue/green?
cards.a: Canary routes a small percentage of traffic to the new version and gradually increases it, with automatic rollback on errors. Blue/green switches all traffic at once and offers instant rollback by switching back.

cards.q: What is a shadow deployment?
cards.a: A copy of production traffic is routed to the new model, but its predictions are never shown to users — it lets you compare outputs offline with zero user risk.

cards.q: When should you choose SageMaker Pipelines over Step Functions for orchestration?
cards.a: When the workflow is end-to-end ML: data, train, evaluate, register, deploy. Choose Step Functions when the workflow spans non-ML services.

cards.q: What does a ConditionStep do inside a SageMaker Pipeline?
cards.a: It branches the pipeline based on a metric threshold, such as AUC above 0.85, routing to model registration or a failure path.

cards.q: What does BYOC mean in the context of SageMaker?
cards.a: Bring Your Own Container — packaging custom training or inference code in Docker so SageMaker can call it through a standard interface.

cards.q: Which Git workflow suits continuous ML retraining better, trunk-based development or Gitflow?
cards.a: Trunk-based development — frequent commits to a shared main branch with strong automated testing, versus Gitflow long-lived branches.

cards.q: What distinguishes an agent from a fixed workflow?
cards.a: An agent decides its next actions at runtime; a fixed workflow follows predefined steps.

cards.q: How do a SageMaker Model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint differ?
cards.a: The Model identifies serving artifacts and execution settings; the configuration describes deployment resources; the endpoint is the running deployment using a configuration.

cards.q: How is an endpoint changed when its deployment configuration is immutable?
cards.a: Create a new endpoint configuration and update the endpoint to use it.

cards.q: Which API submits an S3 input reference to an asynchronous inference endpoint?
cards.a: InvokeEndpointAsync.

cards.q: Which SageMaker inference option in the guide handles a request up to 1 GB with processing up to one hour?
cards.a: Asynchronous inference.

cards.q: When is on-demand Serverless Inference a useful fit?
cards.a: Infrequent or unpredictable requests with idle periods, when the workload can tolerate cold starts and fits supported limits.

cards.q: What does Serverless Inference Provisioned Concurrency buy?
cards.a: A warm baseline of execution capacity that reduces cold-start delays, with a corresponding baseline cost.

cards.q: Where are asynchronous inference inputs and results stored?
cards.a: The request references input in S3, and results are written to S3.

cards.q: How can an asynchronous inference caller learn that a request completed without continuous polling?
cards.a: Use the configured success or failure notification path, such as Amazon SNS.

cards.q: Why can Batch Transform avoid the idle charges of a persistent endpoint?
cards.a: It provisions a job to process an available dataset, writes the results, and releases its resources when finished.

cards.q: What does BatchStrategy MultiRecord do in Batch Transform?
cards.a: It packs multiple records into a request to the inference container.

cards.q: Which option fits scoring an entire customer database every night when no user waits for an individual response?
cards.a: Batch Transform.

cards.q: Which option fits unpredictable individual requests with large inputs when callers can wait for a result?
cards.a: Asynchronous inference.

cards.q: What does SageMaker endpoint data capture record for later monitoring?
cards.a: Selected inference inputs and outputs in S3, according to the configured capture settings.

cards.q: When can a multi-model endpoint reduce hosting cost?
cards.a: When many compatible models have too little individual traffic to justify separate endpoint resources.

cards.q: How does a caller identify a model on a multi-model endpoint?
cards.a: Use the TargetModel request parameter.

cards.q: Why can the first request to an infrequently used model on a multi-model endpoint be slower?
cards.a: The model may need to be downloaded and loaded before it can serve the request.

cards.q: What resource-isolation trade-off comes with sharing a multi-model endpoint?
cards.a: Models share serving resources, so one model's demand or memory use can affect others.

cards.q: When does a multi-container endpoint fit better than a single shared model-serving container?
cards.a: When independent models need distinct containers or frameworks while sharing endpoint infrastructure.

cards.q: What does direct invocation of a multi-container endpoint do?
cards.a: It sends a request to a selected container rather than passing it through every stage.

cards.q: Which request parameter selects a container for direct invocation?
cards.a: TargetContainerHostname.

cards.q: What is an inference pipeline?
cards.a: A sequence of serving containers, such as preprocessing, prediction, and postprocessing, executed for each request.

cards.q: How can an inference pipeline reduce training-serving preprocessing skew?
cards.a: It can deploy the fitted preprocessing together with the model so requests use the intended transformation path.

cards.q: Are multi-model endpoints supported on Serverless Inference in this guide?
cards.a: No.

cards.q: What do inference components add to endpoint model placement?
cards.a: Explicit per-model resource requirements and independently scalable model copies.

cards.q: Why deploy a model from an approved Model Registry package version?
cards.a: It ties deployment to a reviewed version with associated artifacts and evaluation evidence.

cards.q: What distinguishes AWS Inferentia from AWS Trainium by primary purpose?
cards.a: Inferentia targets inference; Trainium primarily targets training.

cards.q: Why can't an arbitrary unprepared model simply be placed on Inferentia?
cards.a: It must use a supported execution path and be compiled for AWS Neuron hardware.

cards.q: Which optimization primarily targets the delay of bringing model weights into service?
cards.a: Fast model loading.

cards.q: What does hardware-specific model compilation optimize?
cards.a: The model's execution for a particular target accelerator or hardware environment.

cards.q: What is the main trade-off of model quantization?
cards.a: Lower memory and potentially faster computation through reduced precision, with possible quality loss that must be measured.

cards.q: Which dimensions should be checked after an inference optimization?
cards.a: Task quality as well as latency, throughput, and cost.

cards.q: How does speculative decoding accelerate generation?
cards.a: A smaller draft model proposes tokens and the target model verifies them, reducing expensive target-model work when proposals are accepted.

cards.q: Why does poor agreement between draft and target models reduce speculative-decoding benefits?
cards.a: Many proposed tokens are rejected, so drafting adds work without enough useful accepted output.

cards.q: What token-level compatibility is required by the speculative-decoding setup described in the guide?
cards.a: A shared tokenizer and vocabulary between the draft and target models.

cards.q: What does SageMaker Inference Recommender help choose?
cards.a: Instance and endpoint configurations based on measured latency, throughput, and cost.

cards.q: If CPU usage is high while the GPU is mostly idle, what should be investigated before buying a larger GPU?
cards.a: CPU-side preprocessing, data delivery, or other work that is starving the accelerator.

cards.q: What is the latency trade-off of dynamic request batching?
cards.a: It can improve throughput, but requests may wait while a batch is assembled.

cards.q: What does a target-tracking scaling policy try to maintain?
cards.a: A selected utilization or load metric near its configured target.

cards.q: How does step scaling react to a threshold breach?
cards.a: It changes capacity by a configured amount associated with the magnitude of the alarm breach.

cards.q: Which scaling approach fits a known daily traffic surge?
cards.a: Scheduled scaling, so capacity can be prepared before demand arrives.

cards.q: Why can scaling cooldowns that are too short cause problems?
cards.a: Capacity can oscillate as the system repeatedly reacts before earlier scaling changes settle.

cards.q: Why is maximum endpoint capacity both a cost control and a reliability constraint?
cards.a: It caps resource spending but also limits how much demand the deployment can absorb.

cards.q: What additional hosting abstraction is required for the real-time scale-to-zero path described in the guide?
cards.a: Inference components, together with the required zero-minimum scaling configuration.

cards.q: How do requests behave while a real-time endpoint is waking from zero capacity in that setup?
cards.a: They can fail while capacity is being provisioned; they are not automatically queued like asynchronous requests.

cards.q: What load unit is useful when scaling inference-component copies for generation workloads?
cards.a: Concurrent requests per model copy.

cards.q: Which signal naturally fits scaling asynchronous inference capacity?
cards.a: Backlog size per instance, because requests wait in a queue.

cards.q: Who manages the instance-count scaling of an on-demand serverless endpoint?
cards.a: The service; the user configures supported controls such as maximum concurrency rather than an instance fleet.

cards.q: What is the basic blue/green deployment pattern for an endpoint update?
cards.a: Prepare replacement capacity, shift traffic to it, and retire the previous capacity after the update is accepted.

cards.q: How does canary traffic shifting differ from all-at-once shifting?
cards.a: Canary sends a limited portion first and observes it before moving the rest; all-at-once shifts the traffic together.

cards.q: How does linear traffic shifting differ from a single canary step?
cards.a: It moves traffic through multiple incremental steps with observation periods between them.

cards.q: What is the purpose of a deployment baking period?
cards.a: To observe the new deployment for problems before advancing the rollout or retiring rollback capacity.

cards.q: What must exist for SageMaker deployment auto-rollback to detect a bad update?
cards.a: Configured CloudWatch alarms that identify failure conditions.

cards.q: Why are endpoint deployment alarms insufficient to establish model correctness?
cards.a: They may detect errors or latency regressions without detecting plausible but incorrect predictions.

cards.q: Does a shadow variant's prediction become the response returned to the production user?
cards.a: No. The production variant serves the response while the shadow receives copied traffic for comparison.

cards.q: Which test fits observing a new model on real traffic without exposing its predictions to users?
cards.a: Shadow testing.
